## What Is an Employer of Record in Argentina


[An Employer of Record (EOR)](https://www.bolto.com/global-hr) is a third-party company that hires workers on behalf of another business. In Argentina, the EOR becomes the legal employer for your Argentine team members, taking on responsibility for payroll, tax withholding, social security contributions, and compliance with local labor law.


You retain full control over the day-to-day work: setting tasks, managing performance, and directing the employee’s output. The EOR handles the legal and administrative side so you never need to register a local entity in Argentina.


Here’s why that matters in Argentina:


- Argentine labor law is layered and protective, with strict rules around termination, severance, and mandatory benefits that vary by collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and industry.
- Setting up a local legal entity typically takes several months and requires ongoing administrative overhead.
- An EOR lets you hire compliantly from day one, without waiting on entity registration or local legal counsel to get up to speed.


In short, an EOR gives you a compliant path to[hire in Argentina](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-international-global-hiring-expansion-guide) without the time and cost of going it alone.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Argentina


Argentina has a detailed legal framework governing employment, and getting it right matters before you make your first hire. Here is what you need to know. This is general information, not legal advice, so consult an employment lawyer for your specific situation.


### The Employment Contract Act


The[Ley de Contrato de Trabajo (LCT)](https://iclg.com/practice-areas/employment-and-labour-laws-and-regulations/argentina/) is the cornerstone of Argentine labor law. It covers everything from working hours and leave entitlements to termination procedures and severance calculations. Most employees fall under its scope, though specific industries may have collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) that layer additional obligations on top.


### Key Compliance Requirements


- Working hours are capped at 8 per day and 48 per week, with overtime paid at a 50% premium on weekdays and 100% on weekends and holidays.
- Employees are entitled to a 13th-month payment, known as the aguinaldo, paid in two installments each year in June and December.
- Statutory vacation ranges from 14 to 35 days annually, depending on the employee's length of service.
- Severance pay is calculated at one month's salary per year of service, based on the highest salary earned in the last year.
- Both employer and employee contribute to Argentina's social security system, with employer contributions running approximately 26% to 28% on top of gross salary depending on company size and category (ARCA, 2026).


Collective bargaining agreements are widespread across sectors like manufacturing, retail, and tech. In many cases a CBA applies to a given role, so it is worth confirming with a qualified advisor before setting compensation.

Setting up a local entity gives you direct control over your Argentine operations, but[the process is slow and expensive](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-international-global-hiring-expansion-guide) . An EOR lets you hire in Argentina without forming an entity at all. Your team member works for you day-to-day; the legal and administrative burden sits with the EOR.

## FAQ


### Can I hire in Argentina without setting up a local entity?


Yes. An Employer of Record (EOR) becomes the legal employer for your Argentine team members, handling payroll, tax withholding, social security contributions, and compliance with local labor law while you retain full control over day-to-day work. This lets you hire compliantly from day one without waiting months for entity registration or maintaining ongoing administrative overhead in Argentina.


### Employer of Record Argentina vs local entity: which is cheaper upfront?


An EOR is far cheaper upfront. Setting up a local entity in Argentina typically costs an estimated $10,000 to $20,000 in initial costs (a rough range that varies with legal, accounting, and registration fees) plus an estimated $3,000 to $5,000 per year in ongoing administrative expenses, and the registration process takes 3 to 6 months. An EOR eliminates setup costs entirely and allows you to onboard your first hire within days to weeks, making it the more cost-effective option for small teams or companies testing the Argentine market.


### What are the mandatory employer contributions in Argentina?


Employer social security contributions in Argentina run[approximately 26% to 28%](https://www.afip.gob.ar/relaciones-laborales/empleadores/aportes-y-contribuciones.asp) on top of gross salary, depending on company size and category (ARCA, 2026). You’re also required to pay a 13th-month salary (aguinaldo) in two installments each June and December, plus statutory vacation that ranges from 14 to 35 days annually depending on length of service. Severance is calculated at one month’s salary per year of service when terminating an employee, based on the highest salary earned in the last year.


### How long does it take to hire someone in Argentina through Bolto?


Bolto typically delivers a first candidate shortlist within 72 hours of posting a role through its local recruiter network. Once you’ve made your hiring decision, EOR onboarding completes in as little as 48 hours, with employment contracts drafted in accordance with Argentine labor law and all payroll and compliance infrastructure set up automatically. This is substantially faster than the 3 to 6 months required to register a local entity before you can legally onboard your first employee.


### Do collective bargaining agreements apply to my Argentine hire?


Potentially. Collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) are widespread across sectors like manufacturing, retail, and tech in Argentina, and they can layer additional obligations on top of the baseline Labor Contract Law (Ley de Contrato de Trabajo). A CBA often applies to a given role and industry, and CBAs commonly set wage bands, overtime rates, vacation entitlements, and termination procedures that override standard employment terms, so it is worth confirming with a qualified advisor before setting compensation.
